name_ar: أم سلمة هند بنت أبي أمية
role: Witness to key events of early Islam
summary: Umm Salamah (RA), born Hind bint Abi Umayya, was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and one of the most learned and long-lived of the Mothers of the Believers. She made the Hijrah to Abyssinia and then to Madinah before her first husband's death, and she was known for her wisdom, beauty, and exceptional memory. She narrated a large number of hadith and lived to witness the events of Karbala, dying in Madinah around 62 AH.
biography:
Hind bint Abi Umayya ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumiyyah — known as Umm Salamah — was born in Makkah around 596 CE. Her father Abu Umayya ibn al-Mughirah was among the wealthiest men of the Quraysh, earning the name 'Zad al-Rakib' (Provision of the Traveler) for his renowned generosity to traveling companions. She came from the distinguished Banu Makhzum clan, known for its warriors and nobles among the Quraysh.

Hind accepted Islam early, along with her first husband Abu Salamah Abdullah ibn Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi (RA), who was a foster brother of the Prophet ﷺ. They were among the first emigrants to Abyssinia in approximately 615 CE, seeking refuge under the Negus from Quraysh persecution. After returning to Makkah, they later undertook the Hijrah to Madinah. The journey was marked by hardship: when Abu Salamah set out for Madinah, his wife and infant son Salamah were forcibly separated from him by her clan. Umm Salamah spent approximately a year separated from her husband and son before she was finally allowed to travel to Madinah, a journey she undertook largely alone until accompanied by Uthman ibn Talhah. Ibn Hisham in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah preserves this account, and it became one of the most-cited examples of the sacrifices made by early Muslim families in the cause of the faith.

Abu Salamah (RA) was seriously wounded at the Battle of Uhud in 3 AH. Although he appeared to recover, he died in Rajab 4 AH from the effects of his wounds, leaving Umm Salamah a widow with four young children: Salamah, Umar, Zaynab, and Durrah. When Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) proposed to her on behalf of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA), she declined. The Prophet ﷺ then proposed to her himself. She expressed concern about her age, her children, and her jealous temperament. The Prophet ﷺ reassured her, and they married in Shawwal 4 AH. Her marriage to the Prophet ﷺ ensured that her four children were raised within the Prophet's household.

Umm Salamah was renowned for her intelligence and her willingness to offer counsel. One of the most celebrated episodes in her life occurred at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah in 6 AH. When the Prophet ﷺ instructed the companions to slaughter their sacrificial animals and shave their heads after the terms of the treaty were signed — terms that many companions felt were unfavorable — the companions initially hesitated, stunned by what they perceived as a setback. It was Umm Salamah who advised the Prophet ﷺ to go out himself and perform the acts, knowing the companions would follow his example without needing further instruction. The Prophet ﷺ acted on her counsel, and the companions immediately followed. This account is recorded by al-Bukhari (Kitab al-Shurut) and is one of the most frequently cited demonstrations of wisdom among the Mothers of the Believers.

She was also among those about whom the Quran spoke directly. When some female companions raised the question of whether the Quranic address to believers included women, Allah revealed verses specifically naming both men and women as recipients of divine address (Quran 33:35), an event that Umm Salamah is credited with prompting through her question, as recorded by al-Tabari in his Tafsir and by al-Tirmidhi.

Umm Salamah was an exceptionally prolific narrator of hadith. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Vol. 2) that she narrated approximately 378 hadith. She transmitted hadith in a wide range of subjects: prayer, fasting, marriage, divorce, inheritance, and personal conduct of the Prophet ﷺ. Her narrations are found in all six major hadith collections.

After the Prophet's death, Umm Salamah lived in Madinah and remained a living scholarly reference for the community. She lived to an advanced age — al-Dhahabi places her death at approximately 84 years old — dying in Madinah around 62 AH (681 CE), making her among the last surviving Mothers of the Believers. She was buried in the Baqi' cemetery. Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Vol. 8) and Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in al-Isabah both regard her as one of the greatest women scholars of the first generation of Islam.

key_events.event: First Hijrah to Abyssinia with husband Abu Salamah
Returned to Makkah; later made Hijrah to Madinah, suffering family separation on the journey
Widowed after Abu Salamah (RA) died; married the Prophet ﷺ later that year
Witnessed the death of the Prophet ﷺ
Died in Madinah; buried in al-Baqi' — one of the last surviving Mothers of the Believers

notable_traits: Deep wisdom and practical intelligence — pivotal counsel at al-Hudaybiyyah
One of the most prolific female hadith narrators (~378 narrations)
First Hijrah to Abyssinia; endured extended separation from husband and son during Hijrah to Madinah
Long life as a living scholarly reference for the companions and their students
Known for a forthright and occasionally jealous temperament — she acknowledged this openly to the Prophet ﷺ
